A new poll takes the temperature on the Mass. governor's race — and all 9 ballot questions | WBUR News

Editor's Note: This is an excerpt from WBUR's daily morning newsletter, WBUR Today. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox, sign up here. We have an October surprise in this fall's election in Massachusetts. Shawn Oliver, the Republican nominee for lieutenant governor, suspended his campaign yesterday, after he was arrested on DUI charges following a crash late Saturday night in New Bedford. Oliver's name will still be on the ballot alongside his running mate, GOP gubernatorial candidate Mike Minogue. However, Minogue said Sunday that he would ask for Oliver's resignation if he's elected.That's a big if, based on the latest polling:State of the race: With just over two weeks until the election, a new poll shows Gov. Maura Healey with a commanding lead over Minogue. The UMass Amherst/WCVB poll released this morning shows Healey, the Democratic incumbent, with 57% support among likely voters, compared to 32% for Minogue. The poll surveyed 800 respondents between Oct. 5 and Oct. 12, before last week's debate and Oliver's arrest. The margin of error was 4.2%. It comes after several other polls this fall showed Healey with a comfortable lead.Perhaps most intriguingly, the poll also asked voters about how they plan to vote on all nine of the ballot questions before them this fall. Here's a look:🟢 Question 1 on expanding the state's public record law had 84% support in the poll, including 55% who said they'd definitely vote yes.🟡 Question 2 on allowing public defenders to unionize had 53% support, with 19% opposed and 14% undecided. Another 14% said they still didn't understand the ballot question. (To that 14%, we say: read our "Law & Order"-themed explainer.)🟡 Question 3 on all-party primaries had 49% support, still ahead of the 39% opposition. But the portion of those opposed has crept up a little since the last UMass poll in August, as more incumbent elected officials rally against it.🟢 Question 4 on Election Day voter registration is holding steady with 67% support, compared to just 26% opposition.🟢 Question 5 on the state's revenue cap/tax rebate law looks pretty likely to pass, with 58% support in the poll and 20% opposition. Another 21% said they were still undecided or don't understand the question. (Ahem: explainer.)🟢 Question 6 on creating a dedicated nature conservation fund is sitting pretty with 70% support and just 19% saying they're likely to vote no.🟢 Question 7 on allowing single-family homes on small lots had 65% support in the polls and just 21% opposed.🔴 Question 8 on repealing legal recreational marijuana sales is facing an uphill battle, with just 31% support. Meanwhile, the poll found 61% opposed to toppling the industry, which was created a decade ago via ballot question.🟢 Question 9, which is a referendum, asks voters if they want to uphold the state's 2024 gun law. And in the poll, it seems most do: 70% said they're likely to vote "yes" to uphold the law (including 49% who said definitely). Twenty-one percent said they'd probably or definitely vote no. 	Go deeper: The UMass poll also includes numbers on other statewide races, word clouds for Healey and Minogue and questions about the ballot question process itself. Here are the toplines and crosstabs.Wait, wait: The MBTA's new Red Line trains have been hit with another delay. Nearly half of voters in pre-election poll say Mass. has gotten worse over 4 years


                                    Many respondents to a new poll believe Massachusetts has become a worse place to live over the past four years and they still favor keeping incumbent Gov. Maura Healey in the corner office over her Republican opponent.More than 42% of respondents to a new Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll released on Tuesday said they thought Massachusetts has become “a little” or “significantly” worse over the past four years and 40% said the state has stayed the same. More than 52% of respondents said they felt like Massachusetts was heading in the right direction.More than 58% of respondents said they’d favor reelecting Healey over tapping her GOP opponent Mike Minogue, who earned 36% of respondents’ backing. Healey led Minogue 56-31 in a UMass Amherst / WCVB poll released on Monday.
More than 34% of respondents in the Suffolk/Globe poll said Healey has performed better than expected throughout her first term. About 35% said she has done worse than expected.When it comes to who respondents view as responsible for the state of Massachusetts’ economy, Healey (34%) and President Donald Trump (more than 33%) are almost tied. Almost 35% of respondents said the state’s economy is “fair” and more than 38% called it “good” or “excellent.” More than 23% said the Bay State economy is “poor.”Throughout this election cycle, Healey has continuously bashed Trump and tried to connect him to Minogue, who has donated to Trump and other Republicans. Minogue has tried to distance himself from the president by avoiding using his name and appealing to voters in the center of the political spectrum.About 60% of respondents said they would not, or be less likely to, vote for a Republican candidate who has voted for or supported Trump. Almost 31% said it makes no difference to them.About 21% of respondents said that they had never heard of Minogue, a first-time candidate and former CEO of Abiomed, and 1.6% said they didn’t know Healey. More than 56% of respondents who know of Healey have a favorable opinion of her. More than 28% of respondents said they had a favorable view of Minogue.The poll surveyed 500 registered voters from Oct. 14 through Oct. 17 and has a 4.4% margin of error.
In a rare moment of agreement, Healey and Minogue have both called for a suspension of the state’s gas tax as prices at the pump have risen. Eleven percent of respondents said gas prices were their greatest source of financial stress.Also, while temperatures are dropping and energy prices are rising, utility/heating bills were the most common financial strain respondents listed with almost 23% saying it was their greatest fiscal burden.Other poll resultsThe poll found respondents favored all of the state’s constitutional officers seeking reelection.More than 54% said they’d vote to reelect Democratic Attorney General Andrea Campbell over her Republican challenger Michael Walsh, who earned around 28% of respondents support.Secretary of State Bill Galvin, a Democrat seeking a record ninth term, received almost 67% of respondents’ support over his Republican contender Anne Brensley, who earned more than 21% of respondents’ backing. Brensley originally ran for lieutenant governor but was knocked off that ballot as a result of allegedly fraudulent signatures and switched to running to become the state’s elections chief.Democratic Treasurer Deb Goldberg beat her Republican opponent Elizabeth Dionne in the poll (58% to more than 24%) as she is seeking a fourth term.Democratic Auditor Diana DiZoglio led her Libertarian opponent Al Ozonoff (more than 64% to 15%) in the poll. DiZoglio is the only constitutional office holder not facing a Republican opponent.U.S. Sen Ed Markey, who was first sent to Washington D.C. as a congressman in 1976, held a comfortable lead of 60% over Republican John Deaton’s almost 31%. Like Minogue, Almost 45% of respondents said they had never heard of Deaton and 75% of those who had held an unfavorable opinion of him.Ballot questionsAround 21% of respondents said they plan to vote “yes” on Question 8 to essentially repeal the state’s recreational marijuana laws and about 71% said they were against abolishing the decade-old industry that was established through a ballot question. Also, more than 60% of respondents said they had never purchased cannabis from a dispensary.On the other repeal question going before voters, more than 57% of respondents also said they’d like to keep the state’s 2024 gun law, saying they would vote yes on Question 9.Question 1, which subjects the governor’s office and Legislature to the state’s public records law, was also popular with more than 62% of respondents saying they would vote for it. Question 4 that proposes allowing Election Day registration also earned more than 59% of respondents’ support. Another question earning support from respondents was Question 2, which allows public defenders to unionize with about 56% saying they’d vote “yes.”The margins were close on other questions: Question 5 changing the cap on state revenue collections and making taxpayer rebates likelier (40% yes and almost 38% no); Question 7 allowing single-family homes to be built on smaller lots (about 41% yes and 40% no); Question 3 to create an all-party primary election system (about 47% yes and 41% no); and Question 6 proposing to create a fund for natural resource conservation from taxes collected on sporting goods (almost 49% yes and 39% no).

Lamar Cook, former Maura Healey staffer facing gun and drug charges, now accused of SNAP fraud


                                                                                                                                        
                                                                

  
      
    
        



  
    
                                      
                          
            
    
      

      
      
      

                
    By

    Lamar Cook, a former staffer for Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey who was fired after his arrest on cocaine and gun charges last year, has been arrested again. This time, Cook is facing federal charges for alleged Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) fraud.Cook, 46, is the former deputy director of the governor's western Massachusetts office. He was fired in November 2025 after being arrested on state charges. Prosecutors said at the time that Cook allegedly had cocaine delivered to a state building in Springfield where he was working.  On Wednesday, U.S. Attorney for Massachusetts Leah Foley announced federal charges against Cook. He is charged with one count of SNAP fraud and wire fraud.Cook appeared in federal court in South Boston Wednesday afternoon.Despite the judge calling the allegations "distasteful," Cook was able to leave the courtroom on personal recognizance following his arraignment.Prosecutors say Cook violated bail on his state charges and will try to have it revoked in a Springfield courtroom on Thursday. Cook did answer any questions from reporters as he left the courthouse.
    
    
                                    
      

      
          
        
        
                  LaMar D. Cook (right) appears with his defense attorney, Kedar K. Ismail, in Hampden County Superior Court on March 6, 2026. 
        
                  
            
                Brooke Hauser/The Boston Globe via Getty Images

                          
              
      
    
  Prosecutors said Cook was making a $130,227 year while working for Healey and received $22,374.29 for accrued vacation time when he was fired. The state later "realized an error" in paying Cook for the accrued vacation time, and unsuccessfully tried to reverse the direct deposits.

    
    
The state was unable to get the money back because Cook did not have enough money in his accounts.Lamar Cook federal chargesThe U.S. Attorney said Cook's bank account held balances of about $13,000 in January 2026 and $8,800 in April 2026.Prosecutors say that Cook's mother won $1 million in the Massachusetts Lottery in early 2026. She made payments to Cook totaling about $12,000 between May and June 2026.On April 6, 2026, Cook applied for SNAP benefits and allegedly claimed zero income, less than $100 in his bank account, and said he was living in a two-person household with only himself and his child.

    
    
    
Cook allegedly failed to disclose that his fiancée and her mother lived with him at his Springfield home. In addition, investigators say his fiancée was making more than $80,000 as an employee of Springfield Public Schools.After applying to the program, Cook received nearly $550 per month in SNAP benefits. Prosecutors said he used them regularly at grocery and retail stores and also during a trip to Disney World in Florida this past July. U.S. Attorney calls allegations "simply egregious" If convicted of SNAP fraud, Cook faces up to five years in prison. A wire fraud conviction would mean a sentence of up to 20 years."The alleged conduct is simply egregious. SNAP benefits are intended to put food on the table for struggling families who cannot make ends meet, not for those who allegedly hide income to circumvent the financial requirements, much less travel to Disney World," Foley said in a statement Wednesday.She called it "disturbing" that the state couldn't stop the alleged SNAP fraud from happening and could not recover the $22,000 it mistakenly paid Cook for his vacation time.During an event on Wednesday, Healey was asked about the latest charges against Cook."Good. That's a federal program. Those are federal taxpayer dollars. And I'm glad that the U.S. Attorney's office has taken action," Healey said.

    
    
    
Healey is currently running for re-election. Her opponent, Mike Minogue, released a statement following Cook's arrest."Maura Healey appointed this man. This is a failure at every level. Families in this state are cutting back at the grocery store while this administration can't even track its own payroll. Governor Healey is about to spend a record-breaking $298 billion over her four-year term, and Cook's case proves we can no longer afford to let her hide what's going on with the numbers," Minogue said.

Opinion | Globe endorses Governor Maura Healey for reelection

In a state with a healthy Republican Party, this might have spelled disaster for the Democratic governor, Maura Healey. But this is Massachusetts, and so Healey is ahead of her Republican rival, Mike Minogue, by formidable margins in most polls. Massachusetts voters’ exceptionally dim view of the Republican president is surely one reason: A recent Suffolk University poll found that 7 in 10 voters rate Trump unfavorably. Get College TownA weekly newsletter packed with insights about higher ed from Globe journalist Hilary Burns.Enter EmailBut Healey deserves credit as well for guiding the state through these turbulent times. She has proposed aid to soften federal cuts to universities, worked to buffer immigrant communities from Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids, and maintained food assistance to families cut off from federal support during a federal government shutdown.The first-term governor’s defiance of the Trump administration can seem performative at times. But on balance, her determination to stand up to White House bullying has been the right thing for Massachusetts. For that reason and others, the Globe editorial board endorses her for another four years in office. Beyond resisting Trumpism, Healey has shown the ability to govern boldly. During her first years in office, before the return of Trump, she made housing her top priority, working with the Legislature to enact a sweeping $5 billion plan that aimed to provide funds for housing construction, reduce costs for renters, permit new kinds of affordable housing units, and ease regulations that had slowed development. It was a sweeping, important plan that seems to have lost some of its urgency in the past two years. She asserts that the state is on the way to building 100,000 of the more than 220,000 units experts say it needs to address its shortage. With four more years in office, we hope that Healey will return to the crisis with renewed commitment. It is the surest way to make Massachusetts more affordable. Healey’s election-year proposals to address the rising costs of health care and energy — not all of them successful — demonstrate an understanding that voters are struggling financially. Should she win another term, she should make concerted, long-term efforts to moderate prices in both areas. She also needs to attend to what appear to be shortcomings in state oversight of nursing homes, as underscored in a recent Globe Spotlight series.Most significantly, we hope that she pushes the balky Legislature into addressing the state’s economic malaise with greater urgency. Once a powerhouse of entrepreneurship and tech innovation, Massachusetts has slipped to near the bottom of the states in forming new businesses and creating private-sector jobs, a recent Boston Globe series showed. As the country prepares to move into the post-Trump era, Beacon Hill will need to do more than sloganize about affordability or blame Washington for the state’s economic woes.Healey’s Republican opponent, Mike Minogue, a West Point graduate and businessman who made a fortune in the medical devices industry, has brought some good ideas to the table. He has called on Healey to opt into the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program created by the Trump administration and called on the state to expand the number of charter school seats — policies supported by this board. He has also been right to urge the governor to rein in state spending and ease more of the regulatory burdens that stifle business creation and new construction. He reasonably supports — as does Healey — nuclear power as an efficient source of energy at a time when solar and wind are not sufficient to meet the state’s rising needs. And while his assertion that high taxes are the root of most economic problems can feel glib, he is not wrong that the state’s tax code needs fixing. But Minogue has yet to flesh out a detailed tax reform plan that might have the vaguest chance of passing in the Democratic-dominated Legislature. And his insistence that cutting “waste and fraud” will balance the state budget suggests a less than full understanding of the complex programs that eat up much tax revenue.Other parts of the Minogue agenda strike us as simply wrongheaded. Most notable is his pledge to stop enforcing the MBTA Communities Act that requires municipalities to allow denser housing near mass transit lines. The law, if imperfect, has also been an important tool for addressing the state’s housing shortage. Perhaps most disappointing about the Minogue campaign has been the Minogue campaign itself. Though he entered the race promising to challenge Healey’s handling of the economy, he has spent much of his time and immense resources — his campaign is largely self-financed — focusing on examples of what he considers waste and corruption, most prominently the state’s plans for a $2 billion courthouse in Springfield. This board has also questioned the skyrocketing cost of that courthouse, along with ethical lapses in Healey’s administration. But in treating the courthouse as a core campaign issue, Minogue has shortchanged his strongest argument: That he represents an alternative vision for growth and prosperity. Instead he has often sounded like he is running for auditor.Healey, to be sure, has also run a less than inspiring campaign, working overtime to accuse Minogue of being a MAGA functionary, based largely on his contributions to Trump and fund-raising for JD Vance in 2024. In reality, Minogue has mostly kept the president at arm’s length while also arguing that he would be better positioned to win back some of the federal aid Trump has withheld from Massachusetts. His argument is not implausible. But it is not enough to warrant an endorsement from this board. Healey has not always been the ambitious and visionary leader this great state deserves. If she wins, we will call on her to bring the same energy she brings to fighting Trump to finding Massachusetts solutions to Massachusetts problems. But she is the right choice for this difficult chapter in the Massachusetts story, one capable of important achievements in a second term. Massachusetts voters should give her that chance.Editorials represent the views of the Boston Globe Editorial Board. Follow us @GlobeOpinion.

Maura Tracy Healey (born February 8, 1971)[1] is an American lawyer and politician serving as the 73rd governor of Massachusetts since 2023. A member of the Democratic Party, she served as Massachusetts Attorney General from 2015 to 2023 and was elected governor in 2022.
Hired by Massachusetts Attorney General Martha Coakley in 2007, Healey served as chief of the Civil Rights Division, where she led the state's challenge to the federal Defense of Marriage Act. She was then appointed chief of the Public Protection and Advocacy Bureau and then chief of the Business and Labor Bureau, before resigning in 2013 to run for attorney general in 2014. She defeated former State Senator Warren Tolman in the Democratic primary and Republican attorney John Miller in the general election. Healey was reelected in 2018.[2] She was elected governor of Massachusetts in 2022.[3]
In 2014, Healey became the first openly lesbian woman elected attorney general of a U.S. state and the first openly LGBTQ person elected to statewide office in Massachusetts.[4] In 2022, she became one of the first two openly lesbian women and the joint-third openly LGBT person elected governor of a U.S. state, as well as the first woman elected governor of Massachusetts.[5][6]
Early life and education[edit]
Healey was born on February 8, 1971, at Walter Reed Hospital, in Bethesda, Maryland.[7] When she was nine months old, her family moved to Hampton Falls, New Hampshire, where she was raised. Healey has four younger siblings.[8] Her mother was a nurse at Lincoln Akerman School in Hampton Falls; her father was a captain in the United States Public Health Service and an engineer. After divorcing, her mother sold her wedding ring to pay for a backyard basketball court.[7] Healey's stepfather, Edward Beattie, taught history and coached girls' sports at Winnacunnet High School. Several of her grandparents and great-grandparents were born in Ireland.[9]
Healey attended Winnacunnet High School,[10] and majored in government at Harvard College, graduating cum laude in 1992. She was co-captain of the Harvard Crimson women's basketball team.[11] After graduation, Healey spent two years playing as a starting point guard for a professional basketball team in Austria, UBBC Wüstenrot Salzburg, now called BBU Salzburg.[12][13] Upon returning to the United States, she earned a Juris Doctor from Northeastern University School of Law in 1998.[14]
Healey began her legal career by clerking for Judge A. David Mazzone of the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts, where she prepared monthly compliance reports on the cleanup of the Boston Harbor and assisted the judge with trials, hearings, and case conferences. Healey subsequently spent more than seven years at the law firm Wilmer Cutler Pickering Hale and Dorr LLP, where she worked as an associate and then junior partner and focused on commercial and securities litigation.[15]
She also served as a special assistant district attorney in Middlesex County, where she tried drug, assault, domestic violence, and motor vehicle cases in bench and jury sessions and argued bail hearings, motions to suppress, and probation violations and surrenders.[15]
Healey (right) and Massachusetts Attorney General Martha Coakley at a July 8, 2010, press conference on the Massachusetts v. U.S. Dep't of Health & Human Servs. lawsuit challenging the Defense of Marriage Act
Hired by Massachusetts Attorney General Martha Coakley in 2007, Healey served as chief of the Civil Rights Division, where she spearheaded the state's challenge to the federal Defense of Marriage Act. She led the winning arguments for Massachusetts in the country's first lawsuit striking down the law.[16]
In 2012, Healey was promoted to chief of the Public Protection and Advocacy Bureau.[17] She was then appointed chief of the Business and Labor Bureau.[18]
As a division chief and bureau head in the Attorney General's Office, Healey oversaw 250 lawyers and staff members and supervised the areas of consumer protection, fair labor, ratepayer advocacy, environmental protection, health care, insurance and financial services, civil rights, antitrust, Medicaid fraud, nonprofit organizations and charities, and business, technology, and economic development.[15][18]
Attorney General of Massachusetts (2015–2023)[edit]
Healey's official attorney general photo, 2015
In October 2013, Healey announced her candidacy for attorney general. Coakley was retiring from the office to run for governor. On September 9, 2014, Healey won the Democratic primary by 126,420 votes, defeating former State Senator Warren Tolman, 62.4% to 37.6%.[19]
Healey's campaign was endorsed by State Senators Stan Rosenberg, Dan Wolf, and Jamie Eldridge.[20] It was also endorsed by Northwestern District Attorney David Sullivan, Holyoke Mayor Alex Morse, Fitchburg Mayor Lisa Wong, and Northampton Mayor David Narkewicz.[21][22] Organizations that endorsed the campaign include the Planned Parenthood Advocacy Fund of Massachusetts, MassEquality, the Victory Fund, and EMILY's List.[23][24][25][26] Healey wrote an op-ed in the Worcester Telegram and Gazette on upholding the Massachusetts buffer zone law, which she worked on at the Attorney General's Office.[14] She also authored an op-ed in The Boston Globe outlining her plan to combat student loan predators.[27][28][29]
Healey defeated Republican nominee John Miller, an attorney, in the general election, 62.5% to 37.5%. Upon taking office, she became the United States' first openly lesbian state attorney general.[30][31]
On November 6, 2018, Healey was reelected Massachusetts Attorney General, defeating Republican nominee James McMahon with 69.9% of the vote.[2]
Healey (far right) in 2016 with (left to right): State Senator Karen Spilka, State Rep. Ken Gordon, U.S. Secretary of Labor Tom Perez, and State Rep. John Scibak
Healey's plan to reduce gun violence addresses what she perceives as its root causes. The program includes enhancing the background check system to include information regarding recent restraining orders, pending indictments, and any relations to domestic violence, parole, and probation information. The plan also seeks to track better stolen and missing guns. Healey advocates fingerprint trigger locks and firearm micro-stamping on all guns sold in Massachusetts.[32][33]
Healey's plan for criminal justice reform includes ending mandatory sentences for nonviolent drug offenders and focusing on treatment rather than incarceration.[34]
Healey plans to combat prescription drug abuse and Massachusetts's heroin epidemic by implementing a "lock-in" program. The program will be carried out in pharmacies to identify and track prescription drug abusers and distributors. Her plan includes deployment of new resources to drug trafficking hotspots, improvement of treatment accessibility, and expanding access to Narcan.[35]
Healey's women's rights platform focuses on sex education, expanding access to abortion services in Massachusetts, and ensuring that every woman in Massachusetts has access to abortion, regardless of where she lives, her occupation, or her income.[36] In 2026, Healey signed into law a bill removing all restrictions on abortion.[37][38]
On July 20, 2016, Healey announced her intention to ban the manufacturing of most assault rifles in Massachusetts.[39] In 2021, as a result of this and other "arbitrary and damaging legislation",[40] Smith & Wesson announced plans to relocate its headquarters and much of its manufacturing from Massachusetts to Tennessee. The new factory opened in Maryville, in 2023.[41]
